articles.title: Julia Stiles Reunites With ’10 Things I Hate About You’ Cast, Cries During Heath Ledger Tribute on ‘Dancing With the Stars’
articles.summary: Julia Stiles paid tribute to the late Heath Ledger on Tuesday night’s episode of “Dancing With the Stars.” During Dedication Night, she performed a contemporary routine with her partner Ezra Sosa to “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You”; in the 1999 film “10 Things I Hate About You,” Ledger’s character…
body: In the video package before her dance, she got choked up telling Sousa, “I learned a lot from Heath… It was so easy with him. I have so many great memories. I really wish I could pick up the phone, and be like, ‘Hey dude.'” She added that her response in that scene was real, and she hopes to “recreate the musk for life he had” in that scene.
Hours before the live show, Sousa shared a statement about the routine on Instagram.
Earlier in the week, Stiles opened up to Variety about the emotional rehearsals.

“I know that Dedication Night is emotional, but I thought I was distanced from it enough. Like, oh, it was so many years ago. Something about seeing clips from that movie and images and hearing my voice and hearing his voice is bringing back so many memories. It’s a lot,” she said, noting that she started crying while practicing. “One of the things that we really hope to do as performers is to make people feel something and have people care about the work that you do, and his memory lives on because it was such an incredible performance.”

articles.title: Netflix Chiefs Concede That Slowdown in U.S. Viewing Sparked the Content Leadership Shakeup: ‘We’re Focusing on Execution,’ Ted Sarandos Says
articles.summary: Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters nodded to slowdown in U.S. viewing and ad sales that spurred the radical shake-up of the streamer’s content leadership during Tuesday’s conversation with Wall Street analysts after its third-quarter earnings release.
body: Peters emphasized that “the quality, quantity and variety of viewing remains healthy and it drives our business model. And the best evidence that we’ve got that we’re delivering that value is churn. We’ve got healthy retention in every region,” he said. For the quarter ended Sept. 30, the level of churn improved on a global basis and in the U.S.

“The ultimate determinant of are we delivering that value is the reaction to price changes. And those recent price changes that we did, including in the United States, have gone well. We’ve seen results that are consistent with past changes,” Peters said.
Most of the regions outside the U.S. delivered strong viewing and engagement, he added.

“Our local titles from those regions are driving engagement and they’re driving business growth. And you can see how our business model works here. We specifically highlighted India, which had a strong slate with a couple titles really, really performing. And as a result, view hours in Q3 in India grew 24% on an absolute basis,” Peters said. “They were also up on a per-member basis, all of which drives membership.”

articles.title: Kurosawa Kiyoshi, Shimizu Takashi Among Directors of Disney+, Hulu Japanese Horror Series ‘Night Tales Club’
articles.summary: Kurosawa Kiyoshi and “Ju-on” director Shimizu Takashi are among the seven filmmakers behind “Night Tales Club,” a six-part Japanese supernatural anthology series set to premiere on Disney+ and Hulu in January 2027.
body: Kurosawa, whose credits include “Cure” and “Wife of a Spy,” and Shimizu, known for “Ju-on” and “The Inugami Family,” each take one episode. So do Katayama Shinzo (“Gannibal,” “The Human Vapor”), Sode Yukiko (“Aristocrats,” “All the Lovers in the Night”), Sakashita Yuichiro (“I Can’t Cry With Your Face,” “Blonde”) and Nakamura Yosuke (“Higuma!!,” “Poison Girl”). Nakajima Kenji (“The Naked Director,” “Tokyo Swindlers”) directs the Hojo sequences.
“As the original author of these stories, I feel an enormous sense of surprise and joy that they will soon be available on screen to scare audiences around the world.” Sawamura said.

The show joins a growing lineup of Japanese series on the streamer. Disney+ already carries “Gannibal,” in which a police officer stumbles on something sinister in a remote village, and “Land of Tanabata,” about a college student with an apparently pointless power who looks into a murder. Lighter fare includes cross-cultural romantic comedy “Merry Berry Love” and comedy variety show “The One Shot.”

articles.title: Access: Horror Virtual Film Festival Sheds Light on Disability by ‘Centering Ableism as the Horror Rather Than Disability’
articles.summary: When Ariel Baska traded their 15-year career teaching Latin for the film industry, they were instantly faced with a series of unexpected guardrails. “I found that all of these doors were closed to me because I could not literally walk in the front door,” Baska tells Variety.
body: The festival runs online from Oct. 4 to Nov. 1 with a large slate of films from emerging filmmakers, as well as a series of panels and filmmaker Q&As. Baska and co-director Heather Petrocelli focused their festival on the horror genre because of the fact that “ableism” and “disabled and disfigured bodies have been at the heart of horror from the beginning.”

The lineup is separated into three blocks of programming: Edibles, The Body Keeps the Score and Dead Darlings. Among the titles featured in this year’s festival is Lee Cleaveland’s “Everhand,” where a one-armed farmer orders a mysterious machine, and he and his wife must face off with a company rep in order to reclaim their humanity. Another is Charlie Gillette’s “Tal,” which translates to ‘mask’ in English, which is a claustrophobic meditation on immigrant identity and familial expectations. “A Fermenting Woman” from Priscilla Galvez follows a peculiar chef and fermentation expert as they prepare a career-saving meal using a very special ingredient.
Petrocelli and Baska’s goal in curating the festival lineup was to find films that align with their mission and reclaim disability’s role in the genre.

articles.title: Christina Applegate says she was wrongly diagnosed with MS
articles.summary: She said in a Tuesday release of her Messy podcast that she was not happy about the new information and her symptoms have only "gotten worse".
body: Christina Applegate thought she was living with multiple sclerosis (MS) for five years, until recently discovering she had been given a wrong diagnosis.
The actress, known for hits like Anchorman and Married With Children, said she was "not happy at all" about the news and in tears when she found out.
"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said in an episode of her Messy podcast released on Tuesday. "If anything, I've gotten worse."

The two-part episode, co-hosted by Jamie Sigler, ends a recent break she took to process the information. An investigation into what has been causing her debilitating symptoms - which she experiences daily - will begin next week.

articles.title: ‘We’ll keep doing this if people pay us!’ The cast of TV hit Ghosts on making a movie – and maybe a caveman spinoff
articles.summary: As the haunters of Button House hit the big screen with a plot about an escaped phantom, we hear how the team just missed each other too much – and why grunting Robin may get his own show.
body: When the final episode of Ghosts was aired in December 2023, the sitcom felt as if it had reached a definitive conclusion. The show’s central relationships, between Charlotte Ritchie’s Alison and the ghosts who haunt her tumbledown inherited manor house, were neatly tied up, as they encouraged her to sell the place to a hotel developer. It was a tearjerker of an episode for the millions of people who watched it, as well as for the cast and crew behind the scenes.

“We had stopped the series with genuinely no intention of coming back,” explains the show’s co-creator Mathew Baynton, who also stars as the callow romantic poet Thomas. “We were all in tears on the last day of filming,” he says, now perched on the uncomfortable end of a chaise lounge in a London hotel suite.
“I was so upset that it finished,” adds Lolly Adefope, who plays the excitable Kitty, from the better structured end of the chaise. “It was like being at a party and you guys were leaving.”
“It was a clear ending, and the guys felt like they had fully explored all of the characters,” says director Simon Hynd, “but I did notice a look of regret in some of their eyes.”

articles.title: Explosive births, talking foxes and the devil in a trenchcoat – the Sitges fantastic film festival in all its creepy glory
articles.summary: Olivia Colman goes vulpine, Rupert Grint’s newborn is a monster and Joko Anwar makes a warmhearted violent ghost story set in an Indonesian prison. If I’d ever wanted children, the films showing at the 59th edition of the International Fantastic film festival of Catalonia in the coastal town of…
body: The theme was celebrated in an evil-kiddy exhibition at the Miramar Cultural Centre, marking the 50th anniversary of Narciso Ibáñez Serrador’s “fantaterror” classic Who Can Kill a Child?, some of which was filmed in Sitges itself. The expo traced the subgenre from 1956’s The Bad Seed, via Rosemary’s Baby and The Exorcist, to this year’s Nightborn, in which poor Rupert Grint, as the hapless husband, is no match for the developing folk-horror bond between his depressed wife, their newborn “child”, and the spooky forest surrounding their house. Finnish director Hanna Bergholm, in her introduction, confessed it was inspired by her experiences of motherhood. Only up to a point, one hopes.

Postpartum depression reared its head again in Mutter: The Diary of a Mother from Turkish director Alphan Eşeli, which begins with a father taking one look at his newborn offspring and fleeing into the woods. Hazar Ergüçlü’s terrific central performance keeps the focus on the social and economic plight of being a single parent, even when your baby resembles the one in Eraserhead.

articles.title: Comedy Trio Please Don’t Destroy Take Their Act to J.Crew for New Suiting Campaign
articles.summary: The campaign makes use of their talents beyond being just pretty faces: "We take suiting seriously" pairs still photography shot by Luke Gilford with a comedy short penned by the trio and Brady Lees.
body: The fashion brand tapped New York-based comedy trio Please Don’t Destroy — comprised of writers and performers Ben Marshall, John Higgins and Martin Herlihy, who rose to fame on Saturday Night Live — to front its newest campaign to shine a spotlight on fall suits. But it makes use of their talents beyond being just pretty faces: “We take suiting seriously” pairs still photography shot by Luke Gilford with a comedy short directed by Herlihy and penned by the trio and Brady Lees.

“J.Crew has a long history of helping people find their first suit,” said J.Crew’s chief marketing officer Julia Collier. “With Ben, John and Martin, we wanted to bring some personality and humor to that experience. They took the idea of a day in the J.Crew Suit Shop and made it entirely theirs, while showing how versatile and well-fitted our suits are.”

As for those still shots, photographer and filmmaker Gilford shot the guys in New York’s Financial District in a range of styles and poses meant to evoke the “energy and attitude” of the city in the 1990s. Gilford’s work has been featured in The New York Times, Vanity Fair, GQ and Vogue.

articles.title: Tom Cruise’s Digger is a commercial flop – but also the perfect climate film for our time
articles.summary: The movie follows Digger Rockwell, whose drilling triggers a vast iceberg that’s five times the size of Washington DC. Digger, the new Alejandro González Iñárritu film, is bombastic, misanthropic and an epic, critically savaged flop. It is also the near-perfect climate change film for our era.
body: Digger Rockwell, the eponymous protagonist played by Tom Cruise, is a bluntly caricatured Texas oilman blase about the environmental ruin of his drilling, even as it triggers a disastrous splitting of the Arctic ice sheet. This causes a vast iceberg, five times the size of Washington DC, to barrel towards Europe and threaten a devastating tsunami.

Much like this impending disaster and the real-world retreat of glaciers and coral reefs, though, the mere act of watching Digger has become a forlorn race against time. The box office failure has been resounding, and Digger’s time on the big screen has been brief.

Facing a predicted $245m loss – the lavishly made film took $8m in its first weekend in the US before dropping 60% for its second – Digger was yanked from more than 2,500 theatres across the US ahead of its third week. Scrambling to find a single cinema showing Digger, I had to resort to spending a Thursday lunchtime with just two other ticket-buying patrons at a major Manhattan venue.
points: The movie follows Digger Rockwell, whose drilling triggers a vast iceberg that’s five times the size of Washington DC.
Digger, the new Alejandro González Iñárritu film, is bombastic, misanthropic and an epic, critically savaged flop.
It is also the near-perfect climate change film for our era.

articles.title: Lance Oppenheim Bribed Robert Pattinson With 200 Zyn Canisters to Star in ‘Primetime’
articles.summary: The actor eventually agreed to portray Chris Hansen in the film, which chronicles the intense production, ethical dilemmas and media sensationalism behind 'To Catch a Predator.'
body: It’s no secret that it took some persuading to get Robert Pattinson to portray Chris Hansen in Lance Oppenheim ‘s Primetime. However, the director is revealing just how he bribed the actor to take on the role.
Pattinson initially joined the film only as a producer, but Oppenheim recently told Vulture that he used Pattinson’s Zyn addiction to help convince him to play the To Catch a Predator host.

Following the special delivery, Oppenheim also dropped off the latest version of the Primetime script with a letter that began, “Dear Chris Han-Zyn.” Pattinson eventually agreed to take on the lead role.
“It was like LeBron [James] making the announcement that he was joining the Heat,” the director added.
